h1: The 6 Best Ring Alternatives of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six video doorbell alternatives to Ring from Tapo, eufy, Reolink, Blink and more, compared on power, resolution and price.
summary: The Tapo 2K is the best Ring alternative: 2K video, battery power and a chime for $25 to $50. The eufy E340 costs more for the same resolution, while the REOLINK PoE removes charging for homes that can run Ethernet. The aosu offers wired or wireless install, and the BOIFUN is the pick for avoiding monthly fees, if the claim holds.
intro: People leaving Ring usually start by comparing resolution, then discover the real fork is power. A battery doorbell mounts in minutes with two screws and goes dark when you forget to recharge it. A wired or PoE one never needs a charge and demands a cable run at the door. Pick the wrong side and either routine or installation turns into the chore.

We reviewed six video doorbells from other brands and scored them on the Primea framework, using listed resolution, power type, price bucket and what each listing really promises. Ring's own models are excluded, since the point is an alternative. Where a listing is thin, as several are, we say so rather than fill the gap with guesses.

products.name: Tapo 2K Wireless Smart Video Doorbell w/Chime
products.verdict: 2K video, battery power and a chime at a low price.
products.description:
The Tapo is a wireless, battery-powered 2K doorbell that ships with an indoor chime, in the $25 to $50 bucket. The chime matters more than it sounds: a doorbell without its own receiver can only ping your phone, which is no help when you are carrying groceries upstairs.

It takes first place because it matches the resolution of the dearer eufy at a fraction of the cost. 2K shows enough detail to read a package label or recognize a face at the step, where plain HD begins to smear. Renters especially benefit, since no wiring is needed.

Buy it if you want the simplest install and a low price. The caveat is battery life: you must recharge it, and the listing does not spell out what features, if any, sit behind a plan.

products.name: eufy Security Video Doorbell E340
products.verdict: A 2K battery doorbell from a security-focused brand.
products.description:
The eufy Security E340 is a battery-powered 2K doorbell from a security-focused brand, in the $100 to $200 bucket. It has the same headline resolution as the Tapo and the BOIFUN, and the same freedom from drilling through a wall for power.

It ranks second because the listing gives you nothing the Tapo does not, at several times the price. The brand and its ecosystem are the argument, and that argument is strong only if you already run eufy cameras or a eufy hub. Absent that, the 2K and battery combination is available much cheaper.

Buy it if you want a doorbell from a company known for home security hardware and plan to expand the system. Skip it if you want the lowest price, since the extra spend buys a name, not a stated feature.

products.name: REOLINK Video Doorbell PoE 2K Wired Outdoor Security Camera with
products.verdict: A 2K doorbell powered over Ethernet, so no battery to charge.
products.description:
REOLINK's PoE doorbell is a wired 2K outdoor camera powered over Ethernet, in the $100 to $200 bucket. Power over Ethernet carries electricity and data down one cable, so there is no battery to charge and no Wi-Fi dropout from a weak signal at the door.

It ranks third because PoE demands an Ethernet run to the doorbell location, and that is the whole installation question. For a homeowner with a conduit or an accessible attic, it is the most dependable design in the group. For a renter, it is close to unusable.

Buy it if you can pull a cable and want a doorbell that never goes offline for charging. Skip it if you rent or cannot run cable: every battery model above it avoids that job entirely.
products.skipIf: You rent or cannot run cable.

products.name: aosu 5MP Ultra HD Wireless & Wired Video Doorbell Camera
products.verdict: A 5MP doorbell that works wired or wireless.
products.description:
The aosu lists 5MP Ultra HD resolution and supports both wired and wireless setups, in the $100 to $200 bucket. The resolution number is the highest on the page, and the dual power option suits buyers who are unsure what their door wiring can support.

It ranks fourth because the Tapo delivers 2K for far less, and the aosu listing offers little detail beyond its megapixels and flexible install. A bigger sensor number does not always mean a better picture, since lens quality and compression matter too, and the listing says nothing on either.

Buy it if you are undecided between battery and wired and want to keep the option open. Skip it if you want the cheapest 2K, because the higher bucket buys flexibility more than stated features.

products.name: Blink Video Doorbell - Head-to-toe HD view
products.verdict: An HD doorbell with a head-to-toe view, wired or battery.
products.description:
Blink's doorbell offers a head-to-toe HD view and runs wired or on battery, in the $25 to $50 bucket. The taller field of view is the useful part: it can frame a package on the step and a visitor's full figure, where a standard wide frame crops one or the other.

It ranks fifth because it lists HD while the Tapo and BOIFUN offer 2K at the same price tier. You give up detail for a familiar name and a flexible power choice. The listing carries few extra features to offset that.

Buy it if you want a simple, low-cost doorbell upgrade and already use Blink cameras. Skip it if 2K resolution matters for reading faces and labels, because it will not match the picks above it on sharpness.

products.name: BOIFUN Video Doorbell Camera Wireless - No Subscription Required
products.verdict: A 2K battery doorbell that says no subscription is required.
products.description:
The BOIFUN is a wireless, battery-powered 2K doorbell whose listing title states that no subscription is required, in the $25 to $50 bucket. On paper its resolution, power and price match the Tapo exactly.

It ranks last because it comes from a lesser-known brand, and the no-subscription promise is a claim in the title that the listing does not back with detail. Cloud storage and smart alerts are where plans usually hide, so a bare statement is not enough. Support and app longevity are also harder to gauge.

Buy it if you dislike monthly fees and want 2K at a low price. Before ordering, confirm in the product description exactly which features work without a plan. Skip it if you want a major brand behind the app.

whatMatters.detail: A battery doorbell is easy to mount and needs recharging, while a wired or PoE model never needs charging but needs cable at the door. That choice shapes your daily routine more than any camera spec. The Tapo, eufy and BOIFUN run on battery, the REOLINK on PoE. Check the power line in the title or specs.

Resolution sets how much detail you can pull from a frame. 2K shows faces and package labels more clearly than plain HD, which matters when you zoom a saved clip. The Tapo, eufy, REOLINK and BOIFUN list 2K, the Blink lists HD, and the aosu lists 5MP. Look for 2K or MP in the title.

Some doorbells lock features such as video history or person alerts behind a monthly plan, which changes the real cost over a few years. Only the BOIFUN states that none is required. Read the full listing for what is included, and check the maker's plan page before you assume free cloud storage comes with the camera.

A chime sounds inside the house when someone presses the button. Without one, you depend on a phone notification, which is easy to miss. The Tapo lists a chime in the box. For the others, check whether one is included or sold separately, and whether it plugs in or works through an existing doorbell transformer.

Wireless suits renters because nothing is wired into the wall, while PoE suits homeowners who can run Ethernet. The aosu and Blink list more than one power option, which helps if you are unsure what your door can support. Match the install type to your cable access before you compare cameras at all.

faq.q: Will these work with my existing chime?
faq.a: The listings do not say. Only the Tapo lists its own chime in the box, so check compatibility with your existing chime on each product page. Confirm the eufy E340 and BOIFUN pairing steps before you count on any indoor sound.

Ignoring power, the spec most listings bury. A battery doorbell like the Tapo needs recharging, and a wired one like the REOLINK needs cable. Decide which maintenance you will tolerate before you compare resolution, since a dead battery means a silent door.
2K shows more detail, and the Tapo proves it need not cost much. The Blink's HD handles simple visitor checks fine. Pay for 2K if you want to read package labels or identify faces from saved clips.

faq.q: How do I install the Reolink?
faq.a: It needs an Ethernet cable run to the door for PoE power, which also carries the data. If you cannot pull cable, choose a battery model like the Tapo or eufy E340 instead, and expect to recharge it every so often.

Only the BOIFUN title states none is required. The others do not say, so check what cloud features cost on the Tapo, eufy or Blink product page before you buy, because cloud history is the usual paid item.

faq.q: Can I use two power modes?
faq.a: The aosu and Blink list wired and wireless or battery options. Confirm the mode in the setup guide, since choosing wired may change how long the camera runs between service and which features are available.

finalTake: For most buyers leaving Ring, the Tapo 2K is the right doorbell: 2K video, battery power and a chime at the lowest price bucket. The eufy E340 only makes sense inside a eufy system. Homeowners who can run Ethernet should pick the REOLINK PoE. Treat the BOIFUN no-subscription claim as something to verify before you buy.
